newsitem.title: USA: Budget pact to extend U.S. debt ceiling.
newsitem.headline: Budget pact to extend U.S. debt ceiling.

text.p: A provision in the budget pact between the Clinton administration and Congress for automatically boosting the debt ceiling through Dec 15, 1999, would remove a potentially contentious issue from next year's election calendar.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, announcing the agreement on Thursday night, said it included an automatic extension in the U.S. debt ceiling to provide enough authority to carry the government's borrowing needs through Dec 15, 1999.

The current legally set debt limit of $5.5 trillion was expected to give the U.S. Treasury borrowing room only through September, 1997, to finance the government's big annual spending deficits. After that, it would have to seek another increase in the debt ceiling, which could become entangled in political manoeuvring before 1998 Congressional elections.
But the change announced by Lott would take the debt ceiling increase out of the politics of the 1998 election.
Economist Lou Crandall of R.H. Wrightson & Associates Inc in New York said it was unclear to him why budget negotiators would have settled on Dec 15, 1999, as the date for a debt-ceiling extension.
"Nothing happens on Dec 15, 1999, to substantially increase or decrease the deficit and borrowing requirements," he said.
Many details of the overall pact, aimed at bringing the federal budget into balance by 2002, have yet to be finalized and written into law, including the specifics of the debt-ceiling rise.
